section.title: Thanksgiving for Philemon's Love
section.sectionRationale: Before Paul asks anything, he gives thanks. He praises Philemon's faith and love, names his gospel partnership, and celebrates how he has refreshed the hearts of the saints. This thanksgiving is not flattery; it is the very ground on which the coming appeal will stand.
section.thesis: Paul thanks God for a faith that works itself out in love, and he holds up the very virtue, a heart that refreshes others, that he will soon ask Philemon to extend to Onesimus.
section.frameNote: One movement: Paul's constant thanks, his report of Philemon's faith and love, his prayer for an effective partnership, and his joy that Philemon refreshes the saints.

verses.text: I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers,
because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints.
I pray that your {{koinonia|partnership}} in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ.
I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have {{anapauo|refreshed}} the {{splagchna|hearts}} of the saints.

koinonia.gloss: Partnership, fellowship, a sharing in common. It describes the deep mutual life believers share in Christ, more than friendship, a joint stake in the gospel and in one another. Paul prays this partnership will become effective, and he will later ask Philemon, on the basis of their partnership, to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself.

anapauo.gloss: To refresh, give rest, relieve, or revive. Philemon has been refreshing the weary hearts of the saints, a track record of practical love. Paul lifts up this very quality, and near the end of the letter he will ask Philemon to refresh his heart too by welcoming Onesimus.

splagchna.gloss: Literally the inward parts, the bowels, used figuratively for the seat of deep affection and compassion, the heart. Philemon has refreshed the splagchna of the saints. The word threads through the letter: Onesimus is Paul's own heart, and Paul asks Philemon to refresh his heart by receiving him.

basic.context: Before Paul raises the hard matter of Onesimus, he tells Philemon how thankful he is for him. He has heard reports of Philemon's real faith in Jesus and his love for God's people, and he prays that this love would keep bearing fruit. He especially notes that Philemon has a way of refreshing tired believers. This is genuine praise, and it is also the very kindness Paul is about to ask him to show to a returning slave.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not empty flattery. Paul is thankful for real things and says so, and by naming Philemon's love and his habit of refreshing others, he gently reminds him of the kind of man he already is. The passage shows us how to encourage people truthfully and to build any hard request on real gratitude.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul prays that Philemon's koinonia, his partnership or sharing in the faith, would become effective. He rejoices that Philemon has refreshed, anapauo, the hearts of the saints. That word for hearts is splagchna, the deep inward affections. Each of these words comes back later: the partnership, the refreshing, and the heart all reappear when Paul makes his plea for Onesimus.
basic.typology: Philemon's love that refreshes the weary is a small echo of Christ, who says to the heavy laden, Come to Me and I will give you rest. The love that flows from faith and revives others reflects the Lord who is the true refresher of tired souls.
basic.christ: The good that Philemon does flows from every good thing that is ours in Christ. His faith is in the Lord Jesus, and his love for the saints is the fruit of union with Christ. Christ is both the source of Philemon's love and the pattern of the refreshing rest that love brings.
basic.god: Paul thanks God, not Philemon, for Philemon's goodness, because God is the giver of the faith and love that Philemon shows. God is the One who works real change in people and delights to be thanked for the fruit He produces in His saints.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 5:6 speaks of faith working through love, exactly what Paul sees in Philemon. Matthew 11:28 has Jesus offering rest to the weary, the refreshing Philemon imitates. First Thessalonians 1:3 shows Paul again giving thanks for faith and love in action.
basic.oneStory: Real faith always works itself out in love that serves others. Philemon's love, praised here, is the seedbed for the reconciliation Paul will ask for, and it shows the shape of the whole Christian life: faith in Christ overflowing into costly love for His people.

context.literary:
Verses 4 to 7 are a thanksgiving, and the shape is the one Paul uses in most of his letters: thanks to God, a report of what he has heard, a prayer, and a closing note of joy. Philemon's version is the shortest and the most precisely aimed. Galatians is the one letter where Paul drops the thanksgiving altogether and writes 'I am amazed,' Galatians 1:6. The presence of this one here is already a message, because Paul has real thanks to give.

The unit has a quiet frame. Verse 5 speaks of love 'for all the saints,' and verse 7 ends with 'the hearts of the saints,' so the word 'saints' opens and closes the passage. Inside the frame stands the prayer of verse 6. The movement runs from Paul's thanks, to what he has heard about Philemon, to what he asks for him, to what that love has already done for others. The thanks and the prayer are held together by the little word 'because' in verses 5 and 7, so that the whole is a single reasoned address and not a string of compliments.

The unit also looks forward. Verse 6 prays for goodness to be fully acknowledged, and verse 14 will speak of Philemon's 'goodness.' Verse 7 speaks of hearts refreshed, and verse 20 will ask 'Refresh my heart in Christ.' Verse 7 ends with the personal address 'brother,' and verse 20 begins its appeal with 'Yes, brother.' The thanksgiving is not a warm up. It plants the three themes of the appeal, good, refreshment and the heart, so that when they come back they come back as things Philemon has already been praised for.

The pronouns reward a look. Almost all of the 'you' in these verses is singular, aimed at Philemon alone. Only the 'ours' of verse 6, 'every good thing that is ours in Christ,' widens to a group. His personal faith is pictured as a gift within a shared wealth.
context.historical:
Letters of the Greek world commonly opened with a prayer or thanks to the gods for the recipient's health and safety. Paul takes that courtesy and fills it with the gospel. The god he thanks is 'my God,' the recipient's health becomes the recipient's faith and love, and the whole is offered through prayer, not formula.

The news that Paul 'hears' about Philemon, verse 5, arrived by messengers. Colossians 1:7-8 shows that Epaphras, who founded the church in Colossae, 'informed us of your love in the Spirit,' and Epaphras is now with Paul, verse 23. So the report is a trusted one. Paul and Philemon have a shared history, since Paul says in verse 19 that Philemon owes him his very self, but they have lived in different towns, and the letters and messengers of friends carry the news between them.

Ancient hospitality was a means by which the early church functioned. There were no church buildings and few inns that a Christian traveller could trust. Travelling workers such as Epaphras, Tychicus, Mark and Aristarchus relied on homes like Philemon's. Romans 12:13 and Hebrews 13:2 urge it, 3 John 5 to 8 praises Gaius for supporting travelling brothers who were strangers to him, and Romans 16:1 and 2 asks the church to assist Phoebe. When Paul says that Philemon has 'refreshed the hearts of the saints,' it is natural to hear in it meals, beds, loans and open doors, though the text itself does not itemize.

The word 'partnership' had a practical edge. In Philippians 4:15 Paul says that no church but the Philippians 'partnered' with him in giving and receiving, and in 2 Corinthians 9:13 the same family of words describes a 'contribution.' Paul is asking that Philemon's sharing should come to full effect, and for a first century believer that included the sharing of goods and homes.
context.canonical:
Thanksgivings built on faith and love run across Paul's letters. Ephesians 1:15 has almost the same words as verse 5, 'your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints,' and Colossians 1:4 has the same phrase with Christ Jesus as the object. In 1 Thessalonians 1:3 it is 'your work of faith, your labor of love,' and in Galatians 5:6 Paul sums up the Christian life as 'faith, expressed through love.' Philemon is a living case of that sentence.

The refreshing in verse 7 belongs to a family of references that includes Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, who 'refreshed my spirit and yours,' 1 Corinthians 16:18, and Titus, whose 'spirit has been refreshed' by the Corinthians, 2 Corinthians 7:13. Onesiphorus 'often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains,' 2 Timothy 1:16. In every case the people who refresh Paul are the same people who risk something to do it.

The refreshment echoes the Old Testament. The Sabbath was meant to refresh the household's lowest members, 'so that your ox and your donkey may rest and the son of your maidservant may be refreshed,' Exodus 23:12, and Deuteronomy 5:14 says it is 'so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do.' Proverbs 11:25 says 'he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed,' and Jeremiah 31:25 promises that the LORD will 'refresh the weary soul.' The one who refreshes the weary is acting as God acts.

In the Gospels Jesus says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, and the Greek verb for 'give you rest' is the same word as the 'refreshed' in verse 7. Philemon's love shows the character of the Lord in whom he trusts.

The partnership of verse 6 is the same fellowship named in Acts 2:42 and 1 John 1:3, which is first a sharing with the Father and the Son, and then with one another.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant Philemon to see himself as he is seen: as a man whose faith and love have already reached the people who needed them. By the time he reaches the request, Philemon has been told that refreshing the saints is just what he does. The request will then ask only for more of the same, and a refusal would have to contradict what Paul has said in front of the church.

Paul also meant to place Philemon's goodness in its right source. The man's faith is 'in the Lord Jesus,' the thanks go to 'my God,' and the good in view in verse 6 is 'ours in Christ.' So when the favour is asked it is not a favour to Paul, but an acknowledgement of something that already belongs to both of them. Philemon is not being invited to be generous from his own stock, but to draw on what he has been given.

And Paul meant the thanksgiving to carry real information. He says in verse 5 that he has 'heard' of Philemon's love. That is an invitation to remember who Philemon is, and it is risky, because it makes a refusal harder. The refusal Paul fears is not a hard word but a failure of love, and he tries to avert it by naming love first.

Finally, he meant Philemon to see that the standard is high. Prayer in verse 6 is that the partnership may 'become effective,' which implies that it has not yet reached its full effect. Even a praised man is asked to grow.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what Paul prayed and what he heard. It does not command anything directly. Philemon is not told in these verses to refresh anyone, and the passage does not say that every believer must show the same pattern of hospitality or that a good report is to be delivered to everyone. The details, the habit of thanksgiving and the news of faith and love, are Paul's own.

What it models is a way of speaking. Paul prays before he asks, names what is good before naming what is hard, and attributes the good to God. A reader can follow that pattern without any literal copying. A leader who must make a difficult request can first remember in prayer the person and what God has done in them.

The passage also invites some care. Praise is not a tool for getting what we want, and the text does not give Paul's thanks as a method of manipulation. The same words would be hollow if they were not true. Paul can say them because he means them, and the lesson for the reader is to look for the real grace in a person before speaking, and to thank God for it.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by praying that Philemon's partnership in the faith may become effective?

views.label: Effective in good deeds and love
views.case: Paul prays that Philemon's shared life in the gospel would keep bearing practical fruit, coming to full effect in acts of love, of which welcoming Onesimus would be one.

views.label: Effective in deepening knowledge of Christ
views.case: The verse ties effectiveness to fully acknowledging every good thing that is ours in Christ, so the partnership grows as Philemon grasps more of the riches he has in the gospel.

debates.bearing: Both readings meet in the same aim: a partnership in the gospel that is alive and working, so that grasping what we have in Christ produces love that acts, exactly what Paul will ask of Philemon.

debates.question: Is Paul's thanksgiving sincere, or is it a bid for goodwill before a request?

views.label: A rhetorical opening to win goodwill
views.case: Ancient letters and speeches often began by securing the hearer's favour, and the thanksgiving in verses 4 to 7 plants the three themes of the appeal. Some readers therefore see it as Paul's skilled preparation, in which praise and the later request are tied together.

views.label: Sincere gratitude that also prepares the way
views.case: Paul gives the same kind of thanks in Romans 1:8, 1 Corinthians 1:4 and Colossians 1:3 with no request nearby, and he drops it in Galatians 1:6 where he has none to give. The thanks reads as a habit of the apostle's heart, not a technique.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals. Paul can mean every word and also see that every word bears on what he is about to ask. The point for the reader is that a request built on true gratitude is honest, while a request built on flattery is not.

debates.question: What is the 'good thing' of verse 6, and what does 'in Christ' mean there?

views.label: Every blessing we possess in Christ
views.case: The BSB reads 'every good thing that is ours in Christ.' On this view Paul prays that Philemon will come to know the full wealth of the gospel, the sort of riches Ephesians 1:3 and Colossians 2:2 and 3 describe, and that sharing the faith will flow from knowing it.

views.label: Every good thing we are to do for Christ's sake
views.case: The Greek phrase is brief and can also be read as pointing to what is done toward Christ or for His sake, so some translations render it that way. On this view Paul prays that Philemon will see all the good that is to be done in the service of Christ, and the appeal that follows is one such good.

debates.bearing: On either reading the practical result is the same. Knowledge of Christ's gifts leads to the doing of good, and verse 14 will name the good Paul has in mind. The BSB's reading puts the stress on grace received, and the alternative puts it on grace passed on.

study.originalLanguages:
Five words or constructions in these four verses carry meaning that the English only partly shows.

First, the word translated 'effective' in verse 6 is energes, the root of the English 'energy.' It is a word of working power. The writer of Hebrews uses it of the word of God, 'living and active,' Hebrews 4:12, and Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 16:9 when he says that 'a great door for effective work has opened to me.' The prayer is that Philemon's sharing in the faith would be a live, working thing, and not only a private conviction. The verb 'may become' implies that the sharing is still arriving at its full measure.

Second, 'fully acknowledge' is epignosis, a word for knowledge that is thorough and personal, a fuller form of the ordinary word for knowing. Paul uses it in Colossians 1:9 and 1:10, where he prays that the Colossians be filled with 'the knowledge of His will' and grow 'in the knowledge of God.' In verse 6 the object is 'every good thing that is ours,' which is the entire stock of what believers have received. The sentence links knowing and doing: partnership becomes effective as the knowledge of good deepens.

Third, 'ours' in verse 6 is plural while nearly every other pronoun in these verses is singular. The footnote to verse 2 notes that 'you' and 'your' are singular throughout the letter except in verses 3, 22 and 25. The single plural 'ours' here includes Paul with Philemon and every believer, and the phrase 'in Christ' states the place where the good is held in common.

Fourth, 'joy and encouragement' in verse 7 uses paraklesis, from the family of the verb parakaleo, which Paul will use for 'appeal' in verses 9 and 10. The man who is encouraged by Philemon's love is about to appeal to him. The same root means 'comfort' in 2 Corinthians 1:3 and 4, 'the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles.' The thanks, the appeal and the comfort share a single word family, so the letter is a coherent piece of encouragement from beginning to end.

Fifth, the verb for 'have refreshed' in verse 7 is a perfect, anapepautai, which describes a completed act with a lasting result. The hearts of the saints did not just receive one kindness; they stand refreshed. It is the same verb that Jesus uses in Matthew 11:28, 'I will give you rest,' and the one in verse 20, where Paul asks for the same refreshment for himself in the form of a command. The sentence ends with the single word 'brother,' set last in the Greek, so that the title Paul will apply to Onesimus is first applied to Philemon in the act of praising him.

typology.type: The Sabbath that refreshes the lowest, Exodus 23:12
typology.fulfillment: Israel's Sabbath was designed so that 'the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident,' and Deuteronomy 5:14 says that servants may rest 'as you do.' The law already tied rest to those under a master's hand. Philemon's refreshing of the saints echoes that care, and Jesus fulfils it by offering rest to all the weary, Matthew 11:28. The type is incomplete because a day of rest returned each week, whereas Hebrews 4:9 speaks of a rest that 'remains' for God's people. Paul does not claim that Philemon's hospitality fulfils the Sabbath. The echo is worth hearing because it shows the same God behind both.

typology.type: The breastpiece and the remembered names, Exodus 28:29
typology.fulfillment: Aaron bore the names of the sons of Israel 'over his heart' as 'a continual reminder before the LORD.' Paul's remembering of Philemon in his prayers in verse 4 is a small pattern of the same priestly care, kept up by an apostle in chains. It is a pattern and not a strict type, since Paul is no high priest. The correspondence is that someone carries the names of others into God's presence. Christ is the fulfilment, for 'He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25, and He bears every believer before the Father without weariness.

typology.type: Faith in a household turned outward, Philemon 5
typology.fulfillment: Philemon's house has become a meeting place for the church. The pattern is the way God's presence has always gathered a people around a dwelling, in the tabernacle, in Israel's households at Passover, and now in a living room. This is a pattern of fellowship and not a proper type, because God's people are no longer tied to a place. The fulfilment lies in Christ, who is 'faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:6, and in the church that is that house. Philemon's love for 'all the saints' reflects what Christ has made of the people He gathers.

study.christ:
The thanksgiving sets Christ at the centre by the way it is built. Philemon's faith is 'in the Lord Jesus,' so Christ is not just the example of the believing life but its object. His love for the saints is the outflow of that faith, which is exactly the order Galatians 5:6 sets out: 'faith, expressed through love.' Faith in Christ is the root, and refreshing others is the fruit.

Christ is also the storehouse. Paul prays that Philemon may fully acknowledge 'every good thing that is ours in Christ.' Ephesians 1:3 says that God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing,' and Colossians 2:3 says that in Christ 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.' The good that Philemon has to share, and the good that he is asked to recognise in another man, comes out of one account. This is why the letter will ask him to receive a slave as a brother. The brother's goodness, too, is in Christ.

The refreshment of the saints is the work of Christ's own heart. 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28, uses the same verb as verse 7, and Jesus describes Himself as 'gentle and humble in heart.' Isaiah 42 pictures the servant who will not break a bruised reed, and Matthew 12:20 applies it to Jesus. When Philemon revives tired believers, he is acting in the manner of the Lord whom he trusts, and the apostle sees in his love an image of Christ.

The partnership of verse 6 is a share in Christ Himself. First Corinthians 1:9 says that God has called believers 'into fellowship with His Son,' and 1 John 1:3 says that our fellowship 'is with the Father and with His Son.' Philemon's koinonia in the faith is the sharing first of all in Christ, and then with the others who share in Him. His partnership with Onesimus, who is soon to be received as a brother, rests on the same Christ.

Finally, Christ is the one who prepares the ground for the hard request. Paul asks no favour that Christ has not already done. Christ took in the useless, forgave debts and received sinners, and the pattern of that welcome is the one Philemon is to follow, Romans 15:7. A caution keeps the reading honest. Philemon is not a figure of Christ, and the refreshment of verse 7 is a human act that images Christ and does not replace Him.
study.god:
The thanksgiving shows God as the giver of what He then receives thanks for. Paul does not thank Philemon; he thanks 'my God.' The faith and love that he hears of in verse 5 are real human works, and they are also what Philippians 2:13 describes, 'it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.' This is how Paul can say in Philippians 1:6 that God 'began a good work' and will 'carry it on to completion.' The teaching of Scripture is that the fruit is both Philemon's and God's, and Paul gives the thanks where they belong.

God is the one who hears prayer. Paul prays 'always' and remembers Philemon by name. The idea that a distant prisoner's prayer could bear on a household in Colossae is a quiet confession that God is near to both and in control of both, and that He moves in a person by means of prayer. Verse 22 says the same from the other side, since Philemon's prayers will help to bring Paul back.

God is the God of all comfort. Second Corinthians 1:3 and 4 calls Him 'the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble.' Philemon's refreshing of the saints is the channel of that comfort, and Paul's joy in verse 7 is the joy of receiving God's consolation through a friend. The Old Testament says the same in Jeremiah 31:25, 'I will refresh the weary soul,' and in Isaiah 40:29, 'He gives power to the faint.'

God sees and remembers service. Hebrews 6:10 says that 'God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name as you have ministered to the saints.' Paul cannot see the whole of Philemon's hospitality, but he trusts that God does.

God is also generous in a way that does not run out. The 'every good thing' of verse 6 implies a store that is greater than the believer knows, and growth in knowing it is part of God's design for His people.

For worship, the passage gives a small lesson. The right response to seeing grace in someone's life is to thank God and not only to praise the person, and then to pray that the grace would go further. It is a way of loving both God and neighbour at once. The passage also steadies us against pride. If our faith and love are God's work in us, then they are gifts to be shared and not trophies to be shown.

crossReferences.note: Almost the same words as Philemon 5, 'ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints,' followed by 'I have not stopped giving thanks for you.' It shows that Paul's thanksgiving here is not a special tool for this letter but the way he habitually prayed for churches and friends.

The thanksgiving for the very town where Philemon lives. Paul gives thanks for 'your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints' and says that Epaphras 'informed us of your love in the Spirit.' This tells us where the report in Philemon 5 came from, and why Paul's news of Philemon is reliable.

Paul gives thanks for 'your work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope.' The pairing of faith and love shows up again with hope added. The verse shows how Paul describes a healthy church: faith that works and love that labours.

'All that matters is faith, expressed through love.' This is the sentence that Philemon verse 5 illustrates. Faith in the Lord Jesus and love for the saints are not two items but one reality, and Paul sees both in the man to whom he writes.

Jesus offers rest to the weary and burdened. The verb for 'give you rest' is the one translated 'refreshed' in Philemon 7. Philemon's refreshing of the saints is a small share in the work of the Lord who is the true source of rest for tired souls.

Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus 'refreshed my spirit and yours as well,' and Paul asks the church to 'show your appreciation to such men.' It shows that Paul names and honours those who refresh the church, and that refreshing was done by particular people with particular costs.

Titus's 'spirit has been refreshed by all of you.' The same verb in the perfect tense appears in Philemon 7. It shows that the refreshing of workers is a recurring thing in Paul's circle, and that it comes from the people who receive them well.

Paul thanks God 'every time I remember you' and speaks of 'your partnership in the gospel.' The shape of the thanksgiving is the same as in Philemon, and Philippians adds the confidence that 'He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion,' the sort of hope behind Paul's prayer for effectiveness.

'God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name as you have ministered to the saints.' It gives the divine side of Paul's praise: the service of the saints is noticed and remembered by God.

The Sabbath was given so that 'the son of your maidservant may be refreshed, as well as the foreign resident.' The law ties refreshment to the lowest members of a household, and Philemon's refreshing of the saints stands in that line, which will soon be tested by a slave in his own house.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with rest. God finishes His work and blesses the seventh day, and a world in which His creatures can rest in Him is the intended shape of things. The fall puts toil, strain and fear in its place, and the rest of the story is, in large part, God's work to give His people rest again. The law makes a small provision of it in the Sabbath, Exodus 23:12, and in the promise 'My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest,' Exodus 33:14. The prophets look for the day when God will 'refresh the weary soul,' Jeremiah 31:25.

Philemon's love fits into that story as an early sign. When Paul says that the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by him, he is naming a small piece of what God has promised to do for His people. The refreshed are tired believers, workers and travellers who have been given a table, a bed and a welcome. It is a sign that the rest of the new age has started to arrive among those who belong to Christ, even while the world is not yet at rest.

The thanksgiving also sits in the story of how God makes a people through faith and love. Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, Romans 4:3, and the new people that come from Abraham's promise are marked by faith in the Lord Jesus and love for all the saints. The word 'all' is crucial. The love that God builds is not selective by rank or status. By the end of the letter, it will have to reach a runaway slave.

The shared partnership of verse 6 is the story's central hope that God would dwell with His people and share Himself with them, a fellowship 'with the Father and with His Son,' 1 John 1:3. The church is the first fruit of that fellowship, and it expresses itself in practical sharing, as in Acts 2:44 to 47.

The story ends with a rest that is complete. Hebrews 4:9 says that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' and Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear, with no more death, mourning, crying or pain. Philemon's refreshing of tired saints is a foretaste of that rest. It sits in the middle of the story as a small, real example of what new creation looks like when it comes into an ordinary house.

sermon.title: Terms of Endearment
sermon.why: The opening message of Begg's series A Study in Philemon covers Philemon 1:1-7, including this thanksgiving, and draws out how Philemon's faith and love and his refreshing of the saints set the stage for Paul's appeal. A faithful, expository treatment of this movement.

quiz.q: Why does Paul thank God before making any request of Philemon?

options.text: He is genuinely grateful for Philemon's faith and love, and this real gratitude grounds the appeal to come.
options.note: Paul builds on true thanksgiving, not flattery, honoring the man Philemon already is.

options.text: It is just a polite formula he uses in every letter.
options.note: Paul does open with thanksgiving often, but here it is specific and genuine, previewing the letter's themes.

options.text: He is buttering Philemon up to manipulate him.
options.note: Paul's praise is sincere and God-directed, not manipulative flattery.

options.text: He had nothing important to say yet.
options.note: The thanksgiving is deliberate and lays the groundwork for the whole appeal.

quiz.q: What two qualities does Paul specifically thank God for in Philemon?

options.text: His faith in the Lord Jesus and his love for all the saints.
options.note: Faith and love, the faith that works itself out in love, are the heart of Paul's thanksgiving.

options.text: His wealth and his generous hospitality.
options.note: Philemon was hospitable, but Paul names faith and love as the deeper qualities.

options.text: His knowledge of Scripture and his teaching gift.
options.note: These are not what Paul highlights here; he praises faith and love.
Paul's thanks center on Philemon's faith and love, not these.

quiz.q: What has Philemon done that especially brings Paul joy?

options.text: He has refreshed the hearts of the saints through his love.
options.note: Paul lifts up this very quality, and will later ask Philemon to refresh his heart by receiving Onesimus.

options.text: He has shown generous hospitality to God's people.
options.note: Philemon was hospitable, yet the text specifically praises how he refreshed the saints' hearts.

options.text: He has given large sums of money to Paul's ministry.
options.note: The text speaks of refreshing hearts, not financial giving.

options.text: He has won many arguments for the faith.
options.note: Paul commends love that refreshes, not skill in debate.

quiz.q: How does this thanksgiving prepare for the appeal that follows?

options.text: The partnership, the refreshing, and the heart that Paul praises here all return when he pleads for Onesimus.
options.note: Paul plants the very words, koinonia, anapauo, and splagchna, that he will later harvest in his appeal.

options.text: It warms Philemon's heart and disposes him kindly before the request.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but more precisely, the very words and themes here return in the appeal.

options.text: It has no connection to the rest of the letter.
options.note: In fact the thanksgiving carefully previews the letter's key themes and words.

options.text: It warns Philemon of coming judgment.
options.note: The tone is warm thanksgiving, not warning.

questions: Paul noticed and named the good he saw in Philemon before asking anything of him. Who in your life could you thank God for out loud this week, and tell them why?
Philemon was known for refreshing the weary hearts of the saints. Whose heart could you refresh right now, and what would that practically look like?
Paul's thanks went to God for the good in Philemon. When you admire something in another believer, do you trace it back to God's work in them?
Real faith shows itself in love. Where is your faith in Christ currently working itself out in costly love for others, and where has it grown quiet?
The love praised here became the seedbed for a hard act of reconciliation. How might the ordinary kindness you practice now be preparing you for a costly obedience later?

translationNotes.note: Partnership in the faith renders koinonia, a shared life and stake in the gospel; the phrase can point both to fellowship among believers and to a shared grasp of all that is ours in Christ.
Hearts renders splagchna, literally the inward parts, used for the deep seat of affection; the same word recurs in verses 12 and 20, tying the thanksgiving to the appeal.
